title: Reframe serving for product teams - onepager
content:
Purpose:
A compact, product-facing positioning brief that reframes inference from a model/infra problem into a product delivery lever. Target audience: PMs, platform/product-engineering, and technical founders evaluating how to ship LLM features with predictable cost, latency and developer velocity.

One-sentence thesis:
Treat serving as a product primitive — the choice of inference platform determines whether you ship quickly or spend months tuning latency, cost, and reliability on margins that matter. Redwood removes that operational drag so product teams can iterate on user experience, not infra.

Why this resonates with product teams (pain statements):
- Shipping delays: teams bogged down by ad-hoc endpoints, inconsistent model behavior across environments, and repeated performance regressions.
- Hidden costs: token, GPU, and ops spend that grows unpredictably during growth and feature experimentation.
- Reliability risk: intermittent latency spikes and fallback complexity that leak into user-facing SLAs and product metrics.
- Fragmented toolchain: different infra for dev, staging, and production forces repeated integration work.

Why Redwood (core narrative pillars):
1) Predictable product economics — not just cheaper models. Redwood gives cost controls (intelligent batching, caching, routing) tied to observable per-route/unit metrics so PMs can forecast feature unit economics before launching.
2) Same API across dev → prod — remove platform friction. The exact same SDK/route config works in hosted, dedicated, or private deployments so teams don’t rewrite wiring at scale.
3) Reliability as a feature — automated fallbacks, model-variant routing, and rollout primitives that make graceful degradation the default, reducing incident load on product teams.
4) Measurable quality guardrails — built-in eval hooks, prompt set regression alerts, and model versioning keep UX regressions visible and actionable.

Tactical proof points (short):
- Customer vignette: A mid-market SaaS moved its answer-ranking flow to Redwood Dedicated and saw median latency drop 42% while predictably halving inference cost per session after enabling prefix caching.
- Feature highlight: Route-level rollout + automatic fallback to a cheaper quantized variant when burst capacity hits a threshold.
- Ops impact: Mean time to recovery cut by 3x because rollbacks and canary rollouts are in the platform.

Competitor gap map (what product teams worry about that competitors miss):
- Pure model vendors focus on the model surface area (quality) but leave serving economics to the user — teams must bolt on orchestration and observability.
- General cloud endpoints promise scale but mix billing and network complexity that erodes per-feature economics.
- Self-hosted runtimes give control but not the integrated guardrails (billing observability, rollout primitives, and routing policy) product teams need to move fast.

Key messaging hooks to test in experiments:
- "Ship LLM features, not infrastructure": emphasize velocity.
- "Know your cost before you scale": emphasize predictable economics.
- "Downtime should be invisible to users, not to your pager": emphasize reliability.

Suggested one-line elevator pitches (A/B test):
A) "Redwood lets product teams ship LLM features with predictable latency and cost, without building a bespoke serving stack."
B) "Turn inference from an ops problem into a product lever — deploy once, observe everywhere, and scale with confidence."

Recommended landing page sections (order):
1) Headline & supporting subline (velocity + economics).
2) Quick bullets: Hosted / Dedicated / Private options + API parity.
3) Product scenarios: Chat, Rerank, Embeddings — with unit economics callouts.
4) Reliability & rollout primitives: short diagram.
5) Proof (customer vignette + metric callouts).
6) Quickstart CTA + SDK snippet.

Objection handling (short):
- "We can host ourselves": ask about long-term ops tax and the need for integrated rollouts, billing visibility, and cost predictability.
- "Public APIs are cheaper": compare unit economics at product scale, and highlight hidden ops and engineering velocity costs.
- "We need air-gapped/on-prem": Redwood Private is the same API with customer-controlled plane and KMS/HSM integrations.

Next steps for GTM:/content owners:
- Run a 2-week messaging sprint with two landing variants (Velocity-first vs Economics-first) and measure CTR and demo requests.
- Create a product one-pager for platform teams that maps specific API calls to product outcomes (latency, cost, reliability).
- Draft a short 3-slide sales playbook for SDRs to triage product-vs-infra buyer signals.

Open questions to resolve in follow-up:
- Which specific customer vignettes do we want to surface (names + metrics)?
- Benchmarks: compile 3 real workload profiles (chat, rerank, embeddings) with Redwood vs competitor unit cost comparison.
- Demo flow: should the demo focus on rollout + fallback or cost forecasting?

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Consider a small interactive calculator to let PMs estimate cost per feature (inputs: tokens/session, QPS, cache hit rate).
- Build a short video showing a canary rollout, an induced model regression, and an automatic fallback to illustrate reliability.

End of brief."
